notes:
I've finished the research, but coverage is uneven. The old verse-by-verse commentaries (Pulpit, Gill, Clarke, Benson, Barnes, Keil & Delitzsch, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Matthew Henry, Whedon) say a lot about vv. 27–29, 34, 47 and 49–51. On the city lists in vv. 35–46 I found very little. I ran out of searches before reaching the netbible.org notes, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. The only Catholic source I found was Haydock (on studylight.org), and I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching for this passage.

## Section 1 – Asher (vv. 27–31)

**v. 27:** Whedon says this Beth-dagon is a different place from the one in Joshua 15:41. It was probably a Philistine colony, and "Zebulun" here means the tribe, not a city. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/joshua-19.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says the name shows that Dagon, the fish-god, was worshipped in the north as well as the south. It also says this Cabul can hardly be the Cabul of 1 Kings 9:11–13, though it was near it, and that a village with that name still stood about four hours northeast of Acre. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joshua-19.html
- Gill notes that Dagon was a Phoenician god with temples in several places in Canaan. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-19.html

**v. 28:** The Pulpit Commentary says "Ebron" is probably the same place as Abdon, the Levite city of Asher in Joshua 21:30, because the Hebrew letters d and r look so alike. It adds that "Great Sidon," like Tyre, was given to Asher but never conquered. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joshua-19.html

**v. 29:** The Pulpit Commentary takes "fortified city of Tyre" to mean the walled city on the mainland. Most commentators, it says, think the famous island city had not been founded yet. It argues that this phrase and "Great Sidon" point to the book of Joshua being early. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joshua-19.html

**vv. 30–31:** Matthew Henry notes that Asher had few famous places. Aphek was where Ahab beat Ben-hadad. The only famous person he names from the tribe is Anna the prophetess (Luke 2). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_019.cfm
- Precept Austin uses Asher as a warning: the tribe was richly blessed, yet when the time for action came, they failed to trust in God and honor His plan. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-19-commentary

## Section 2 – Naphtali (vv. 32–39)

**v. 32:** Bible Hub's chapter overview points out that the order of the lots follows the birth order of Jacob's sons: Simeon (Leah's son) through Naphtali (Bilhah's son), then Dan (Bilhah's son). https://biblehub.com/joshua/19.htm

**v. 33:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say most of these places have not been found. Since Zaanannim was near Kedesh (Judges 4:11), the border must have run from southwest to northeast, up to the sources of the Jordan. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jos/Jos_019.cfm

**v. 34 ("Judah at the Jordan"): the hardest phrase in the passage.** The Pulpit Commentary says these words have caused great trouble to translators and expositors for 2,000 years. The Greek Old Testament (LXX) leaves them out, but no other ancient version does, so they belong in the text. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-34.htm
The commentators offer five explanations:
- **Jair's towns:** Barnes, Keil, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Cambridge Bible say "Judah" means the Havvoth-jair, Jair's towns across the Jordan from Naphtali. These counted as Judah's because Jair descended from Judah through Hezron. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-34.htm
- **A trade link by river (Benson, Methodist):** Naphtali did not border Judah, so the phrase means the two tribes traded with each other along the Jordan. Benson says some saw this as fulfilling Moses' blessing in Deuteronomy 33:23. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/joshua-19.html
- **A copying problem (Clarke, Methodist):** Naphtali certainly did not touch Judah. The difficulty disappears if "Judah" is dropped, as the LXX does, but no Hebrew manuscript supports that. Clarke thinks the wording was probably changed at some point. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/19-34.html
- **A town called Judah (Gill, Baptist):** Gill says the tribe of Judah is not meant, because it was far away. "Judah" was a city. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-34.htm
- **Different punctuation (Whedon, Methodist):** Whedon calls the old translation faulty. "And at Judah" belongs with the western border, and Judah was a town there, perhaps Jehudiyah. A new sentence then says the Jordan formed the eastern border. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/joshua-19.html

**vv. 35–38:** Precept Austin notes that Joshua burned Hazor and that modern archaeology lends support to this biblical account. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-19-commentary
- Kedesh later became one of the cities of refuge (Joshua 20:7). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/

**v. 39:** Bible Hub's overview ties Naphtali's blessing in Deuteronomy 33:23 to Jesus' ministry in Galilee. https://biblehub.com/joshua/19.htm

## Section 3 – Dan (vv. 40–48)

**vv. 40–46:** Matthew Henry notes that Dan, like Simeon, is described by its cities only, not its borders. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_019.cfm
- Guzik names Timnah, Joppa and (after the move north) Dan as notable cities. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-18-19/
- Clarke takes Thimnathah (v. 43) to be the same place as Timnah. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/joshua-19.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says Dan's land was extremely small, but it was also extremely fertile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-47.htm

**v. 47 – what "went out" means:** The Hebrew literally says the territory "went out from them," and the old commentators read it differently.
- **It was lost:** Ellicott says the words "too little" in older English Bibles are not in the Hebrew; the land was partly taken back by the Philistines. Poole links the verb to land "going out" of an owner's hands in the Jubilee laws (Leviticus 25). Gill says Dan lost part of its land when the Amorites drove it into the hills (Judges 1:34). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-47.htm
- **It went beyond its borders:** The Pulpit Commentary follows Masius: Dan's border went far past its first allotment, up to the northern edge of the land. Whedon agrees. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-47.htm ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/joshua-19.html

**v. 47 – when it happened:** Gill, Benson and Poole say the capture of Leshem came after Joshua died (Judges 18). Gill and Benson think Ezra or another inspired writer added the note, and that this does not prove Joshua didn't write the book. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-47.htm

**v. 47 – whether Dan acted well:** Here readers really disagree.
- **Mostly critical:** Ellicott says the Danites chose to kill a peaceful people rather than fight the Philistines and Amorites in their own land. Coffman calls the episode a later apostasy of the tribe (Judges 17–18). Precept Austin's verdict is In a word, it was UNBELIEF. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-47.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/19-47.html ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-19-commentary
- **Mixed or positive:** Bible Hub's teaching notes praise Dan's perseverance and "faith and action." They also say the land was lost through partial obedience and warn about the idol shrine the Danites set up there (Judges 18:30). https://biblehub.com/joshua/19-47.htm
- **Reformed:** The Geneva Study Bible sees the event as fulfilling Jacob's prophecy in Genesis 49:17. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-47.htm

**v. 47 – the place:** Clarke says the phrase "from Dan to Beersheba" comes from this city. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/19-47.html
- The Cambridge Bible identifies it as Tell el-Kadi, "mound of the judge," a name that keeps the meaning of "Dan" (judge). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-47.htm
- **Catholic (Haydock):** The Douay Bible's "Lesem Dan" joins the old and new names together. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/18-7.html

**v. 48:** Gill says the note about Leshem was put here so the whole account of Dan's inheritance would be in one place. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-47.htm

## Section 4 – Joshua's inheritance and the close (vv. 49–51)

**v. 49:** All the commentators agree this shows Joshua's humility. Guzik says Joshua took his share last and only received what the people gave him, which makes him a wonderful picture of Jesus Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-18-19/
- Matthew Henry says Joshua put the common good ahead of himself. He also notes Joshua would not take land without the people's consent. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_019.cfm
- Benson admires the wonderful modesty of this great man. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/joshua-19.html

**v. 50 – "as the LORD had commanded":** No such command appears in Genesis–Deuteronomy, so the commentators guess.
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Cambridge Bible think it was an unrecorded promise like the one made to Caleb. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-50.htm
- Gill suggests either the Urim and Thummim, consulted by Eleazar, or a word spoken to Moses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-50.htm
- Whedon says it came perhaps through the high priest, or more likely to Moses. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/joshua-19.html

**v. 50 – the place:** Gill and Clarke say Timnath-serah was rough, poor ground. Jerome tells how his friend Paula was surprised the man dividing the land chose such a rugged spot for himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-50.htm ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/joshua-19.html
- Barnes rejects the rabbis' explanation of the other name, Timnath-heres ("portion of the sun"), as tied to the sun standing still. He suggests "Timnath-serah" means "remaining portion," because it was the last share given out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-50.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary warns not to confuse it with Timnah in Dan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-50.htm
- Howard, quoted at Precept Austin, notes the city appears in no tribal list, so it seems to have been Joshua's personal property. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-19-commentary

**v. 50 – "he built the city":** Matthew Henry compares Joshua having to build his own home with Christ, who had nowhere to lay his head. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_019.cfm
- The Biblical Illustrator links Joshua asking for the city with Psalm 2:8 ("Ask of me, and I shall give thee the nations"), applied to Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-49.htm

**v. 51:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown call this the formal close of the land division; the leaders and the place are named again because the event mattered so much. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jos/Jos_019.cfm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary notes Eleazar is named before Joshua here, just as in Joshua 14:1. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/19-51.html
- Clarke says that because the lots were cast "before the Lord," no one complained; each tribe took its share from God's hand. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-18-19/
- Guzik adds that each tribe still had to fight to take what God had given. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-18-19/

## How the traditions compare

I didn't find any real disagreement along denominational lines. The splits are over particular verses, and they cut across traditions:
- **v. 34:** Even the Methodist writers disagree with each other: Benson says river trade, Clarke says a copying problem, Whedon says punctuation. Gill (Baptist) says a town.
- **v. 47:** Whether Dan acted in faith or unbelief.
- **vv. 49–50:** The Christ-pictures in Joshua (Henry, Guzik, the Biblical Illustrator) are a style of preaching that crosses traditions, not a disputed doctrine.
